title: The Best Retirement Plans for U.S. Small Business Owners (SEP, SIMPLE IRA)
description: Choosing between Solo 401(k), SEP IRA, and SIMPLE IRA to maximize tax shelters.
content:
Small business owners in the US often neglect their own retirement because they are too busy reinvesting in their company. This is a mistake. The US tax code offers business owners significantly higher contribution limits than standard employees—often allowing you to shelter over $60,000 per year from taxes. However, the 'Alphabet Soup' of account types (SEP, SIMPLE, Solo) is confusing. Choosing the wrong one can lead to lower contribution limits or administrative headaches. This guide breaks down the three best options for entrepreneurs.

Key Takeaways

  • Solo 401(k) (The Gold Standard): Best for owners with no employees (except a spouse). Allows huge contributions ($69k+) and Roth options. Has a loan provision.
  • SEP IRA (The Easy Option): Best for high-income freelancers who want zero paperwork. Only the employer contributes (up to 25% of profit). No catch-up contributions allowed.
  • SIMPLE IRA (The Team Option): Best for small businesses with a few employees. Lower limits ($16k) but easy to administer. Mandatory employer match required.
  • Deadline Awareness: Solo 401(k)s must be established by Dec 31. SEP IRAs can be set up as late as your tax filing deadline (April/Oct).

Why It Matters (US Context)

Unlike W-2 employees who are capped at $23,000 (2025), business owners can use the 'Employer' side of the ledger to contribute profit sharing, effectively tripling the tax-advantaged space available to them.

Plan Comparison Matrix

Which vehicle fits your business model?

1. Solo 401(k) (Individual 401k)

  • Eligibility: Business owner + Spouse ONLY. No other staff.
  • Limit: Up to $69,000 ($76,500 if 50+).
  • Pros: Highest limits at lower income levels. Roth option available.
  • Cons: Form 5500 filing required once assets exceed $250,000.

2. SEP IRA (Simplified Employee Pension)

  • Eligibility: Any business size.
  • Limit: Up to $69,000 (calculated as 25% of compensation).
  • Pros: Easiest setup. No annual IRS filings.
  • Cons: If you have employees, you must contribute the same % to them as you do to yourself (expensive). No Roth option.

3. SIMPLE IRA

  • Eligibility: Under 100 employees.
  • Limit: $16,000 ($19,500 if 50+).
  • Pros: Employees can contribute their own money (unlike SEP).
  • Cons: Employer MUST match 3%. Lower limits than 401(k).

Strategic Selection

  1. The Solopreneur: Open a Solo 401(k). It beats the SEP because you can contribute the $23,000 'Employee' portion even if your profits are low. The SEP requires high profits to hit high contribution numbers.
  2. The 'Side Hustler': If you have a day job 401(k), you can still open a Solo 401(k) for the side gig, but you can only use the 'Employer' profit-sharing bucket (approx 20% of net side income).
  3. The Growing Agency: If you plan to hire 5 people next year, do NOT open a SEP IRA. You will be forced to pay 25% of their salary into their retirement. Start with a SIMPLE IRA or a standard 401(k) with safe harbor provisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I do a Backdoor Roth with these?

A Solo 401(k) does NOT block the Backdoor Roth. A SEP IRA or SIMPLE IRA does block it (pro-rata rule). If you want to do Backdoor Roths, stick to the Solo 401(k).

What is the deadline?

Solo 401(k) plans must be established by Dec 31, even if funded later. SEP IRAs can be established and funded up until the tax filing deadline (April 15 or Oct 15 with extension).

Can I borrow from it?

Only the Solo 401(k) allows loans (up to $50k). IRAs (SEP/SIMPLE) do not allow loans.
